verses.translation_literal: A shiggaion of David, which he sang to YHWH on the words of Cush, a Benjamite.
verses.translation_dramatic: A shiggaion of David, a song he sang to the LORD over the words of Cush, a Benjamite.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a title, and in the Hebrew Bible it counts as the first verse, which is why every verse in this psalm is numbered one higher than in the KJV. Nobody knows what 'shiggaion' means. Rashi reports Menachem's view that it is one of the names of a song, named for an instrument, with Hab 3:1 ('shigyonot') as the parallel, and the rabbis' view that it comes from 'error' (mishgeh). Ibn Ezra reports 'delight' (compare 'always be ravished', Prov 5:19), as Meiri also holds, and gives his own view: a melody that began with the word 'shiggaion', like the tune-names that Spanish poets wrote at the head of a poem. Do not play it as a mood; play it as a label on the page.

'Cush' is a name here (the word also means Nubia), and 'ben-yemini' is a single gentilic, 'a Benjamite', as the KJV renders it. The question is who he is. The Talmud (Moed Katan 16b, as Rashi and Radak report) says Cush is Saul: as a Cushite does not change his skin, so Saul did not change his hatred; Radak adds that it may also mean handsome, like the 'Cushite woman' of Num 12:1. Ibn Ezra rejects this: how could the Lord's chosen be the man of whom the psalm says 'he travails with iniquity' (v. 15)? Radak answers that David said as much to Saul's face (1 Sam 24:13-14), and Meiri thinks the name was veiled out of respect for the king ('curse not the king, even in your thought', Eccl 10:20). The Hebrew does not settle it; keep Cush a man whose 'words' (divrei, also 'matters, affairs') have put David's life at risk.

philological_notes.note: A word in a psalm title of unknown meaning. Menachem (in Rashi) and Radak take it as a kind of song, comparing Hab 3:1; Rashi also gives 'error' (from the root of shagah); Ibn Ezra's own view is the name of a tune.
'On the words of' also means 'on the matter or affair of'; Radak compares Exod 8:8 and Metzudat Zion Num 25:18. Both senses are in play: Cush spoke, and a quarrel arose.
A gentilic written as two words, 'a Benjamite', literally 'son of Yemini'. Meiri: 'because he was of the tribe of Benjamin'.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH my God, in you I have taken refuge; save me from all my pursuers, and rescue me.
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD, my God, in you I have hidden myself. Save me from everyone who hunts me. Pull me out.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens in the middle of a chase, with the first word a name. 'Taken refuge' (chasah) is a physical verb: the image is a fugitive ducking behind a rock or under a wing, and the speaker puts the whole body of it into the perfect tense, 'I have already run to you'. The KJV 'put my trust' is a thinner, churchier phrase that turns an act of running for cover into a state of mind.

Note 'all my pursuers' (kol-rodefai): the enemy is plural here and singular in the next verse. The speaker is one man against a pack. 'Save' (hoshia) is a general word for getting out of trouble; 'rescue' (hatzil) means to snatch something out of an enemy's grip, and Malbim hears the second as already seized, 'after I am caught, pull me out'.

philological_notes.note: 'To take refuge,' a physical flight to a shelter, used of birds under a wing and men behind a rock. It is a completed act, which is why the speaker can ask for rescue on its strength.
'To snatch away'; Malbim distinguishes it from 'save' as rescue from a trap that has already closed.

verses.translation_literal: Lest he tear, like a lion, my life, ripping, and there is no deliverer.
verses.translation_dramatic: Or he will tear at my life as a lion tears, ripping it apart, and no one will be there to pull me free.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Lest' (pen) is a fear clause: the speaker is giving God the reason to hurry. Do not play it as a calm argument. The lion is the king of beasts, and Radak notes that is why the psalm says this of a king (Saul) and not of an ordinary foe. The enemy has switched from plural to singular ('he'), the lion image tightening the pack into one throat.

Two verbs of butchery follow: 'tear' (taraf), used of a predator's kill, and 'rip' (paraq), which means to pull apart or break limbs off, as the same root is used in Exod 32:2 for taking earrings off ears. The KJV 'my soul' is correct as far as it goes, but nefesh is also the throat, the neck, the living person. Hear the lion's teeth at the neck. The last clause, 'no one to deliver', is the reason for the whole cry: in the ancient world a lone man cut off from his clan has no protector, and God is the only one left.

philological_notes.note: To tear apart or break off; Rashi compares Exod 32:2 (stripping earrings off), Metzudat Zion compares Zech 11:16. Ibn Ezra suggests a lion breaking the neck.
Often 'soul', but originally 'throat, neck, breath, living self'. Here it is both the life and the body with a throat the lion goes for.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH my God, if I have done this, if there is wrong in my palms,
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD, my God, if I have done this thing, if there is any wrong on my palms,
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker now takes an oath of innocence, and the sentence is left deliberately unfinished: 'if I have done this, if there is wrong on my hands' with the 'then' held back until verse 6. That is the form of a self-curse in the ancient Near East: you list what you deny and name the penalty for lying. The 'this' is whatever Cush has accused him of; the next verse says what it is.

The KJV 'iniquity' is a church word. The Hebrew 'avel is plain crookedness, injustice, a thing done to somebody, and 'in my palms' (kappai) is the image of the hand held up open to show it is empty. In a world where the right hand carries the sword, you swear by showing it. Meiri hears this as the speaker answering a whisper: that David was plotting against the king.

philological_notes.note: Injustice, crookedness, a wrong done to a person; the KJV 'iniquity' makes it sound like a religious offence when it is a legal one.
'In my palms': the hands as the instrument of deeds and the place where guilt is shown. Ibn Ezra: the palm is what a man strikes and kills with.

verses.translation_literal: If I have repaid [one] at peace with me evil, and [yet] I rescued my adversary for nothing,
verses.translation_dramatic: If I have paid back harm to the man who lived at peace with me, when I even pulled my enemy free, and got nothing for it,
verses.directors_commentary:
Here is the 'this' of the oath. 'The man at peace with me' (sholmi) is literally 'my peace-man': an ally, someone whose shalom he shares; compare 'the man of my peace' in Ps 41:10. Radak says it is Saul: David had been his son-in-law and fought his wars, and Saul repaid good with evil. 'Repaid' (gamal) is the vocabulary of exchange: you give back what you were given. To repay good with evil is the worst treachery an ancient reader could name.

The second half is hard. Radak reads it as an affirmation inside the oath: 'it is not enough that I never repaid my friend with evil; I even rescued those who were my enemies for nothing', as when he held back Abishai (1 Sam 26:8) and in the cave (1 Sam 24:8). On his reading the vav of 'va'achaletzah' is adversative, as in 'no, my lord, but your servants have come' (Gen 42:10), and 'riqam' means 'for nothing, with no gain to me'. The KJV and ASV put the clause in parentheses, and what they render is exactly this affirmative reading ('yea, I have delivered him that without cause is mine enemy'). The others differ. Rashi hears 'chalatz' as 'strip': did I damage his robe, cut the hem of his garment, to ruin and leave him bare? No, I did it to show him he had been in my hand. Meiri hears 'riqam' as 'empty-handed': I let him go without a gift, at worst. Ibn Ezra takes 'riqam' with the enemies, 'those who hate me for nothing', and reports R. Moshe's view that the vav means 'only'. The translation follows Radak.

philological_notes.note: 'The one at peace with me', a friend or ally; Ibn Ezra notes this Qal participle is otherwise rare.
Radak: 'and I rescued', the vav adversative as in Gen 42:10. Rashi: 'strip' (to remove), the hem cut from Saul's robe. Meiri also gives 'send away'. Metzudat Zion: 'draw out'.
'Empty, for nothing'. Radak: the rescue brought him nothing; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion: 'without cause', of enemies who hate for nothing; Meiri: 'empty-handed'.

token_glosses.gloss: my one at peace with me

verses.translation_literal: Let an enemy pursue my life and overtake, and trample to the earth my living, and lay my glory down in the dust. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then let an enemy run me down, and catch me, and grind my life into the ground, and bed my honor in the dust. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the curse that completes the oath: 'if I have done this... then let the enemy...'. Verbs of hunting climb in order: pursue, overtake, trample. The last two images are of a man ridden down: 'to the earth' and 'to the dust' make a pair, with 'life' and 'glory' standing for the two things a man in his world cannot lose, his breath and his name.

'My glory' (kevodi) is the weighty thing, a man's honor and standing; Ibn Ezra and Radak take it as a poetic word for the self (as in Ps 16:9, 'my glory rejoices'), and the KJV 'mine honour' is fair. The verb 'lay down' (yashken) is literally 'cause to dwell', so the enemy makes his honor take up residence in dust, a grim domestic image. The vocal pause 'Selah' falls here, as the oath ends; Radak says it is a raising of the voice in the music, not a word with meaning here.

philological_notes.note: 'My weight / glory / honor'; Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as the self or soul, citing Ps 16:9 and 119:25.
A musical or liturgical marker of uncertain meaning; Radak takes it as a lifting of the voice.

verses.translation_literal: Arise, YHWH, in your anger; lift yourself up against the furies of my adversaries; and awake to me: justice you have commanded.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise, LORD, rise in your anger. Lift yourself above the rage of those who hem me in. Wake, and come to me: you yourself commanded justice.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood flips. Having sworn his innocence, the speaker calls God to battle, using the three verbs by which the ancient Near East woke a sleeping or distant god and roused him to fight: arise, lift yourself up, awake. This is the language of the Ark (Num 10:35, 'Arise, YHWH') and of the divine warrior. The shout 'Arise!' is the loudest word in the psalm.

'The furies' (evrot) is a plural of intensity: 'overflowing rage'. The same word is about God's anger when it overflows; Malbim notes that the psalmist's enemies are those who go beyond the limit. The KJV 'because of the rage of mine enemies' hides that 'lift yourself up' takes 'against' or 'over' them, and that 'my enemies' is not 'enemies' (oyvim) but 'those who press me in' (tzorerai, from the root of tightness, 'siege'). The last clause is blunt: justice is something God has already commanded, so the speaker is not asking for a favor but calling in a debt. The KJV 'to the judgment that thou hast commanded' pushes it into a relative clause. The Hebrew just puts the two beside each other.

philological_notes.note: 'Overflows, furies', from the root 'to cross over'; Malbim distinguishes it from 'af' (anger) as anger that crosses the limit.
'Those who press me in', from the root 'to bind, to be narrow'; the same root as 'tzar', a tight place.
'Awake to me' is an awkward construction. Radak takes it as 'stir yourself on my side, in the judgment you ordered'; Ibn Ezra supplies a missing preposition; Meiri compares Job 41:10.

verses.translation_literal: And an assembly of peoples will surround you, and over it, to the height, return.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the gathered nations ring you round, and above them all take your seat again on high.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture is a court. An 'assembly' (edah) is a gathering, and 'peoples' (le'ummim) are the nations as a body. They stand in a ring round God, and he goes back up to the high place. The verb 'return' (shuvah) does not say that God was ever absent. Meiri gives two senses: withdraw your presence from them (compare Hos 5:15, 'I will go and return to my place'), or go back up to the seat of judgment to judge them.

The word that divides readers is 've'aleha', literally 'and over it'. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'over it': rise above the assembly and show them your strength. Metzudat Zion glosses 'aleha as 'for its sake' (be'avurah), and Malbim and Metzudat David follow, so God should withdraw 'for the assembly's sake' and turn away from it; this is what the KJV's 'for their sakes therefore return thou on high' renders. Both readings are grammatical. Rashi reads it as a plea not to answer the nations if they cry out to be saved. Radak takes the assembly to be Israel's own tribes, who in pursuing the anointed David pursue God himself, and rejects the Christian reading of the verse. Meiri also takes the assembly to be the enemy host. Malbim hears Cush and his company encircling God with accusations. The translation keeps to the court picture and the reading 'over them'.

philological_notes.note: 'An assembly of peoples'. Radak takes it as the tribes of Israel; Meiri as the host of enemies; Rashi as the nations who may cry out to God.
'And over it' (Ibn Ezra: that God be exalted over them) or 'for its sake' (Metzudat Zion: be'avurah; Malbim).
'Return', an imperative. Rashi: go back and sit in your place on high; Meiri: withdraw from them, or sit on the throne of judgment.

token_glosses.gloss: and over it (or: for its sake)

verses.translation_literal: YHWH judges peoples; judge me, YHWH, according to my righteousness and according to my integrity upon me.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD judges the peoples. Judge me, LORD, by my righteousness, by the wholeness I wear.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two verbs for judging stand side by side. 'Yadin' (he judges, governs) is said of God over the peoples; 'shofteni' (judge me) is the imperative, and in this context asks God to find for the speaker and put him in the right. R. Moshe, as quoted by Ibn Ezra, hears it as 'take my case from the one who wronged me' (mechomsi). Ibn Ezra's own view is different and plainer: 'You, LORD, are judge of the earth: judge me by my righteousness, for I did not repay Cush evil.' The speaker is not asking to be inspected for flaws; he offers his conduct as evidence.

'My integrity upon me' (tumi alai): 'tom' is wholeness, a man undivided, and the preposition says 'upon me', not 'in me' as the KJV and Webster have it. Hearing it as something worn is my own reading, and the commentaries do not say it. Metzudat David glosses it 'my integrity that is on me'. Rashi reads the plea as asking God to weigh him by his good deeds and not his sins, and Radak takes 'peoples' to be Israel, with God taking vengeance for David on those who hated him for nothing. Do not play this as boasting.

philological_notes.note: 'Judge me', and here 'vindicate me'. R. Moshe (in Ibn Ezra): 'take my case from the one who wronged me'; Ibn Ezra: 'judge me by my righteousness'.
'According to my integrity upon me': tom is completeness, blamelessness. Metzudat David: my integrity that is on me, so that God passes over the sins.

verses.translation_literal: Let the evil of the wicked come to an end, please, and establish the righteous, and tester of hearts and kidneys, God, righteous.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the evil of the wicked end, I beg you. Set the righteous firm on their feet. For you test the heart and the kidneys, God, and you are just.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two halves of the verse are a wish and a reason. First the wish: 'let it come to an end' (yigmor), a verb of finishing; Rashi gives it as 'ending', and the speaker adds a soft little 'please' (na) that the KJV 'Oh' replaces with a sigh. 'Establish' (tekhonen) is the verb for setting a house on its foundations.

Then the reason, and here the KJV is right to say 'reins'. The Hebrew says 'kidneys' (kelayot), and in the ancient body they are the seat of the hidden inner life, the conscience and the emotions, with the 'heart' as the thinking mind. A god who tests 'hearts and kidneys' sees the plans and the feelings underneath the words. The ASV 'minds and hearts' translates the idea; the KJV 'reins' is an old English word for kidneys that no one now reads. Keep the anatomy, the way the Hebrew does: God's test goes through a man's body.

philological_notes.note: Kidneys, the hidden organs and seat of conscience and secret feeling; KJV 'reins'. Ibn Ezra: 'a figure for hidden things, as the kidneys are hidden'.
'Let it come to an end'; Rashi compares Ps 77:9 and 12:2.
'Establish, set firm'; Meiri takes it as setting the righteous on their base, i.e. his own throne.

token_glosses.gloss: let it come to an end

verses.translation_literal: My shield is upon God, savior of the upright of heart.
verses.translation_dramatic: My shield is held by God, the one who saves the straight of heart.
verses.directors_commentary:
A short, firm verse, and after the storm of the last ones the actor should lower his voice. 'My shield' (maginni) is the armor a soldier holds in front of him; the claim is that God has taken that job. 'Upon God' (al-elohim) is an odd preposition: the shield rests on God, or the burden of the defense rests on him. Radak noticed this: 'why upon? He should have said my shield is God': the answer is that it means 'my reliance is on God'. The KJV 'my defence is of God' reads it as 'comes from God', which the Hebrew does not say, and the BBE 'is my breastplate' turns a possession into a garment.

The 'upright of heart' (yishrei-lev) is the opposite of the crooked; it ties back to 'heart' in the last verse and to 'straight' as an old word for honest. A soldier's shield is only as good as the man behind it, and the verse says exactly that kind of man gets saved.

philological_notes.note: 'My shield rests upon God' (the burden is his); Radak: 'upon' means my reliance is on God; Ibn Ezra: I do not make war, I lean on God.
'Straight of heart', the opposite of crookedness; the heart is where the speaker's claim of honesty rests.

verses.translation_literal: God [is] a righteous judge, and God [is] indignant every day.
verses.translation_dramatic: God is a just judge, and God burns with anger, day in, day out.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first half is calm; the second is not. The Hebrew of 'shofet tzaddiq' can be read two ways, and both have support. 'A righteous judge' (Ibn Ezra, who takes 'righteous' as an epithet of the judge; Rashi, 'you, to judge justly') is the plain adjective. 'Judge of the righteous' (Radak, Meiri, the KJV) makes 'righteous' the one judged: God judges the righteous by his righteousness and the wicked by his wickedness. The translation gives the adjective reading.

The second clause is where the English versions split. 'Zo'em' is a strong word, to be indignant, to denounce, not only 'angry'. The Hebrew gives no object, and the KJV supplies 'with the wicked' (so also Meiri). Radak reads it differently: God judges the righteous, 'and [he judges] the one who rages at God every day', because that man will not turn, which ties to 'if he does not turn' in the next verse; Malbim agrees. For Radak that man is Saul, who scorned God's word, hunted David daily, and swore he would not kill him. Ibn Ezra also notes that 'every day' may belong to the next verse. The YLT's 'He is not angry at all times' follows a reading with 'lo' that is not in this Hebrew. A judge who is fair and furious every day is a frightening thing to say to someone chasing you.

philological_notes.note: To be indignant or to denounce, stronger than 'af' (anger). Metzudat Zion: a matter of anger; Radak: the subject may be the man who rages at God.
'A righteous judge' (Ibn Ezra, Rashi) or 'judge of the righteous' (Radak, Meiri, the KJV): both readings have support.

verses.translation_literal: If not he turns back, his sword he sharpens; his bow he has trodden, and he has made it ready.
verses.translation_dramatic: Unless he turns back. Unless he turns, the whetstone is already singing along the blade, and the bow is bent, drawn taut, and made ready to loose.
verses.directors_commentary:
Verses 13-14 are the hinge of the psalm: the pleading prayer to a judge turns into a vision of the judge armed. The pronoun 'he' is deliberately unmarked, and the old commentators split. Rashi and Meiri hear God sharpening His sword against the man who will not repent; Radak and the Targum hear the persecutor sharpening his own. Play it as a double: the weapon is real, and the audience must wonder whose hand holds it before verse 16 answers them.

Two details the KJV smooths over. 'Bent his bow' is darakh, 'to tread': an ancient archer stepped on the lower limb of a stiff composite bow to string it, so the image is of a man putting his weight into the weapon. And 'lo yashuv' ('if he does not turn') uses the same root, shuv, that returns in verse 17, when the wicked man's mischief 'turns back' upon his head. The man who will not turn is the man whose evil turns on him; the KJV 'turn not' and 'return' lose that echo in the reader's ear. Practically, a sword was whetted before battle; this is a warning that the fight is about to begin, not a threat of delay.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'to tread'. Used of bending a bow because the archer trod on it to string it. The same root gives derekh, 'way'; the bow is 'trodden' as a road is.
'Turn back', here the first use of the root that returns at 7:17 as 'it returns'. Rashi takes the subject as the wicked turning from wickedness.

token_glosses.gloss: and he has made it ready

verses.translation_literal: And for him he has made ready implements of death; his arrows for the burning ones he makes.
verses.translation_dramatic: And for him, for that very man, the instruments of death are laid out. The arrows are shaped in fire, and every one of them has a mark.
verses.directors_commentary:
'For him' (velo) is the stress of the line: whatever is prepared is prepared for this particular man. Metzudat David and Radak (one reading) take it as the wicked man's own fate, 'for his own soul', which sets up the reversal of the next verses. The instruments of death, kheli mavet, are the quiver and bow, blunt and unromantic: a weapon-kit, not a metaphor.

The last phrase is a famous knot. Ledolekim is a participle of dalaq, 'to burn', so the arrows are 'for burning ones' (ASV and BBE: fiery shafts, perhaps flaming arrows wrapped in tow and lit). The KJV 'persecutors' follows Rashi and Metzudat Zion, who connect dalaq to Genesis 31:36, where Jacob says Laban 'hotly pursued' him: the pursuer is one who burns after you. Neither reading is arbitrary and the text likely plays on both; the actors should hear pursuit as heat. The KJV 'ordaineth' also hides a concrete verb, pa'al: to craft, to work with the hands, as a smith does.

philological_notes.note: Participle of dalaq, 'to burn, to be hot after'. Either 'burning' arrows or 'hot pursuers', as in Genesis 31:36; the verse probably holds both.
'Implements of death', the plain term for a weapon set: kli is any tool or vessel.

verses.translation_literal: Look: he labours with wickedness; and he has conceived mischief, and has given birth to falsehood.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look at him. He is in labour with wickedness, heavy with mischief, and what he brings into the light of day is a lie.
verses.directors_commentary:
The imagery turns abruptly from the armoury to the birthing room, and the audience should feel the lurch. A man is pregnant: conception (mischief), labour (wickedness), delivery (falsehood). Radak maps the stages onto plan, speech and deed; Malbim notes the cruel twist that what is born is not the child he planned, a lie that collapses.

The KJV ('travaileth with iniquity') is accurate but its 'travaileth' has gone opaque: it means 'is in labour' and shares a root with 'travel' and 'travail'; modern ears hear journey, not childbirth. The three nouns, aven, amal and sheqer, are near-synonyms for wrongdoing, trouble and deceit, and the Hebrew piles them up like the three stages of the pregnancy. Ancient audiences knew the dangers of labour, so a man in labour with evil is both grotesque and fatal. The hearers also know that the metaphor cuts against the speaker's enemy: his own body will betray him.

philological_notes.note: To be in labour; from chevel, 'pang, cord'. Rashi cites Song of Songs 8:5, 'there your mother was in labour with you'.
Toil, trouble; here the trouble one causes others. Meiri says that next to aven or sheqer it is close to ma'al, 'treachery'.

verses.translation_literal: A pit he dug, and he hollowed it out, and he fell into the pit [which] he made.
verses.translation_dramatic: A pit — he dug it. He dug it deep, down and down, working it hollow in the dark of the earth. And then he fell. He fell into the very pit he made.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the proverb at the end of the three-step image that began in verse 15: conceive, be pregnant, give birth. Now the metaphor changes from the womb to the hunter's field, but the story is the same. The wicked man's scheme turns on its maker. Play it quickly and without relish; the actors who say it should sound like people stating how the world works, not gloating.

The Hebrew piles up verbs: he dug (karah), and he hollowed it out (vayachperehu). Two roots for digging, one after the other, give the sense of effort and care. Radak reads the pair as a doubling of one idea in different words, while Meiri says the second verb means he deepened it. The pit is a hunter's trap, covered over to catch game, and the archaeology of the ancient Near East knows such pits for wild animals and for enemies. Then the punch: the last word, yif'al, 'he makes', is an imperfect with no 'asher' ('which') in front of it, though Hebrew poetry often leaves it out; Ibn Ezra notes the same omission elsewhere in this psalm (v. 12). Meiri, the Targum ('the pit which he made') and the KJV ('the ditch which he made') all read it as a relative clause, and so do we. An imperfect can also be read as ongoing, 'the pit he is making', as though the digger is still at work when he falls; that is possible, but the relative-clause reading is the plainest.

The KJV (7:15) numbers this verse one lower, because it does not count the superscription as verse 1, but its rendering is faithful here. Its 'ditch' for shachat is a small stretch: the word is a pit, the same word used for the trap of Prov 26:27 (Metzudat Zion). Radak and Meiri hear a prophecy in the past tense: the enemy will die by the sword he lifted.

philological_notes.note: A second digging verb after karah. Ibn Ezra takes it as adding depth ('to add to its depth'); Radak reads the pair as one idea said twice. The suffix -hu points back to the pit.

A pit or trap; Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'in a pit', as in Prov 26:27 (koreh shachat). The ordinary word bor in the first half and shachat in the second give the verse a rhyme of sense: the same pit, named twice.
Imperfect of pa'al, 'to make, to do'. With an omitted asher it is a relative clause, '[which] he made', as the Targum and Meiri read it. A durative reading, 'he is making', is possible but secondary.

verses.translation_literal: His mischief turns back on his head, and on his crown his violence comes down.
verses.translation_dramatic: His mischief comes home, and it comes home to his head. His violence falls from above and lands on the crown of him.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verdict, and it is a boomerang. The verb is shuv, 'turn back', the same root as in verse 13 ('if he does not turn'): the one who will not turn is turned upon. The second line adds a verb of falling, yered, 'goes down', so the harm returns and descends like a thrown stone landing. Malbim separates the two halves by anatomy: amal, the thought, comes back to the head, the seat of the plan; chamas, the violence, comes down on the kodkod, the outer scalp.

The KJV 'pate' is a good older word for the crown, but it now sounds comic, and 'violent dealing' is a soft substitute for chamas, which in Hebrew law and prophecy is a heavy word: bloodshed and brutal injustice. Ibn Ezra notes that the verb is 'comes down' because judgment comes from heaven. Retribution here is not a new act of God but the natural, cruel consequence of the trap: he is not struck but returned to himself. The stress should fall on 'his': his mischief, his head, his violence.

philological_notes.note: The crown or top of the head, the part where the hair parts, according to Metzudat Zion.
Violence, wrongful bloodshed, injustice. A strong legal word, not just 'dealing'.

verses.translation_literal: I will give thanks to YHWH according to his righteousness, and I will sing praise [to] the name of YHWH, Most High.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I will give thanks to the LORD, as justly as He has judged, and I will sing to the name of the LORD, the Most High.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the long courtroom and the armoury, the psalm ends in song, and the singer is the one who began in fear. 'According to his righteousness' says that the thanks is measured by God's justice: the psalmist is thanking Him as one who has seen the trap close, and Rashi hears it as thanks when God lets a full judgment fall on the wicked. The tone is quiet and wondering, not triumphant.

The KJV renders the name as 'the Lord', which hides the Hebrew's repeated YHWH (twice in a short verse) and flattens 'name of YHWH Most High' into a stray adjective. 'Elyon, Most High, is an old title, also borne by the Canaanite high god in the surrounding cultures; the psalm claims it for YHWH alone. Ibn Ezra links 'Most High' with the verb 'came down' in verse 17: the judgment descends because He is above. Two verbs of praise, odeh (thank, with the hands lifted) and azamrah (sing with an instrument) frame the response of the body: first lifted hands, then the music.

philological_notes.note: To give thanks, confess; from yad, 'hand', the sense of lifting a hand to acknowledge. Thanks and public confession of praise are the same act.
'Most High', from 'alah, 'go up'. Ibn Ezra sets it against 'comes down' of verse 17.
To sing praise, with music.
